title: Legal Scholars and Lawmakers Challenge Trump’s Basis for Iran War
description_medium: After the United States and Israel began attacks on Iran on February 28, legal scholars and lawmakers questioned the administration’s legal justification. The Guardian reported that officials gave several rationales, including degrading Iran’s military and nuclear capacity and responding to an imminent threat. Experts said military objectives alone do not establish a legal basis for force and that self-defense requires evidence of necessity and imminence. On March 4, the Senate rejected a war-powers resolution 47–53; that vote did not decide the legal question in court.
description_long: The Guardian reported on March 4, 2026, that legal scholars and lawmakers disputed the Trump administration’s basis for the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran, which began on February 28. Officials had cited different aims, including degrading Iran’s offensive and nuclear capabilities, responding to an imminent threat and protecting U.S. interests after Israel prepared to attack. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran posed an imminent threat to the United States. Wells Dixon of the Center for Constitutional Rights argued that military objectives were not themselves a legal basis for an armed attack. International-law scholar Marko Milanovic and former State Department lawyer Brian Finucane said lawful self-defense requires a valid basis, including necessity and imminence; they disputed that those conditions were met. Other lawmakers argued that Iran posed a threat to Israel but not an imminent threat to the United States. The Senate voted 47–53 on March 4 against a war-powers resolution that would have required congressional permission before continuing the campaign. Republicans said Trump had not broken the law and cited presidential commander-in-chief authority. The report documents a contested legal debate and a congressional vote, not a court judgment declaring the war illegal.
evidence_notes: Guardian attributes the illegal-war assessment to named legal experts and lawmakers, while reporting the administration’s imminent-threat rationale and Republican defense. The Senate vote rejected a resolution 47–53; it did not adjudicate legality.
corrected_wording: Adjusted headline to attribute the legal challenge to scholars and lawmakers, and replaced generic catalog impact text with the reported arguments, vote and limits of the claim.

title: Trump Threatens to Urge Unendorsed Candidate to Drop Out of Texas Senate Runoff
description_medium: After John Cornyn and Ken Paxton advanced to a May 26, 2026 runoff for the Texas Republican Senate nomination, Donald Trump said he would endorse one candidate soon and ask the other to leave the race. In a March 4 Truth Social post, Trump argued that the November stakes were too high for the primary contest to continue. Neither candidate had received his endorsement at the time, and Trump did not identify his choice.
description_long: Texas voters sent Sen. John Cornyn and Attorney General Ken Paxton to a Republican Senate runoff after neither candidate won a majority in the March 3, 2026 primary. Their vote totals were separated by just over one percentage point, leaving a second contest scheduled for May 26. The next day, President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that he would soon endorse one of them and would ask the candidate he did not endorse to drop out. He argued the race could not continue because of the stakes for Republicans and the country in November. Trump did not name his preferred candidate in the post. The Texas Tribune reported that Paxton said he would stay in the race even if Trump endorsed Cornyn. The endorsement statement came after Trump had stayed neutral in the primary and while both candidates prepared for a costly runoff. The statement documents Trump’s intention to intervene and his pressure on the eventual non-endorsed candidate; it does not itself constitute an endorsement or show that either candidate withdrew.
evidence_notes: Texas Tribune reports exact March 4 statement, no candidate named, runoff date, close primary result, and Paxton’s stated intention to remain. Later endorsement is outside the event’s March 4 scope.
corrected_wording: Replaced generic consequences with the actual March 4 statement and contemporaneous runoff context; distinguishes promise to endorse from an endorsement already made.

title: Texas Primary Results Set Cornyn-Paxton Runoff and Talarico Democratic Nomination
description_medium: The March 2026 Texas primaries sent Republican Sen. John Cornyn and Attorney General Ken Paxton to a May 26 runoff after both fell short of a majority. State Rep. James Talarico defeated Rep. Jasmine Crockett for the Democratic Senate nomination. The races drew heavy spending and national attention, while Trump stayed neutral in the Senate primary until after the first round. His endorsement and the runoff campaign remained unresolved in the March 4 reports.
description_long: Texas’s March 3, 2026 primaries left several major contests undecided and set up another round of campaigning. Republican Sen. John Cornyn finished narrowly ahead of Attorney General Ken Paxton, but neither received a majority, so they advanced to a May 26 runoff. On the Democratic side, state Rep. James Talarico defeated U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett for the Senate nomination. The Texas Tribune described the Senate primary as a record-setting advertising contest, with nearly $100 million in ad purchases and more than $71 million spent to support Cornyn, according to the media-tracking firm AdImpact. The account also noted that Trump had remained neutral in the first-round contest, though he could still affect the runoff with an endorsement. On March 4, he said he would endorse soon and ask the candidate he did not support to leave the race. Those results made the general-election matchups and Trump’s role in the Republican runoff immediate questions for Texas politics. The accessible material verifies the primary outcomes and the endorsement statement, but not the exact four questions posed by the linked New York Times explainer.
evidence_notes: Texas Tribune supplies the primary results and Trump’s pending role; linked NYT page was not accessible and the packet contains only its headline. This is a supported summary of the same election events, not a reconstruction of all four NYT questions.
corrected_wording: Changed the question-style headline into an event title and used same-election reporting for concrete context. Marked partial because the linked NYT explainer’s four specific questions remain unverified.
exact_blocker: The linked New York Times article’s four questions are not present in the packet and were not accessible. Same-event reporting supports the primary outcomes and Trump’s pending endorsement, but does not establish the full four-question framing.

title: Trump’s Speech Order and Project 2025 Target Federal Responses to Online Election Falsehoods
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to stop unconstitutional limits on speech and requiring the attorney general to review prior federal actions related to online moderation. Project 2025 separately proposed using the FCC and Congress to pressure platforms that limit election-related falsehoods and reducing CISA and FBI work countering them. Those proposals and the executive order are government actions; Meta’s own decision to end U.S. third-party fact-checking was a separate company policy change.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order titled “Restoring Freedom of Speech and Ending Federal Censorship.” The order asserted that the previous administration had pressured social-media companies to moderate or suppress speech and directed the attorney general to investigate federal actions over the prior four years and recommend remedial steps. Project 2025, a separate policy blueprint, proposed that the Federal Communications Commission and Congress use antidiscrimination law against platforms limiting visibility of core political viewpoints, including election-denial content. It also proposed limiting federal agencies’ election-disinformation work and exposing platforms to suits for removing false election claims. The Brennan Center described these proposals as a plan that could intimidate platforms and weaken efforts to counter election falsehoods; they were recommendations, not an enacted rule compelling platforms to carry particular content.

Meta’s January 7 announcement that it would end U.S. third-party fact-checking and move toward Community Notes was a company decision made before Trump signed the order. Reuters reported that Trump welcomed the change and said it was “probably” in response to his threats, but Meta described its own rationale as a shift toward free expression. The order, Project 2025’s proposed measures and Meta’s policy change are related parts of the period’s debate about moderation, but the sources do not establish that Trump legally required platforms to host false claims or eliminated all moderation systems.
evidence_notes: White House order text concerns federal actors and orders AG investigation; Brennan Center describes Project 2025 recommendations as proposals; Meta’s corporate statement and Reuters show the independent platform policy change, announcement date and Trump’s comments. No source proves all moderation systems were eliminated or federally required to carry misinformation.
corrected_wording: Reframed the unsupported claim of completed moderation-system elimination around the signed federal order, distinct policy recommendations and separately attributed Meta decision.

title: ICE Memo Reportedly Planned to End Camp East Montana Contract; Facility Stayed Open
description_medium: On March 5, 2026, The Guardian reported that an internal ICE memo indicated plans to terminate the $1.2 billion contract for Camp East Montana, a detention facility at Fort Bliss in Texas. DHS said no final decision had been made. The report described three detainee deaths and a measles outbreak, but the memo did not establish a closure plan. ICE later replaced the operator and kept the camp open under a new contractor.
description_long:
Camp East Montana, a tented ICE detention facility at Fort Bliss near El Paso, became the subject of closure reports in early March 2026. The Washington Post reported that an internal ICE document showed the agency was drafting a letter to terminate its $1.2 billion contract with Acquisition Logistics LLC. The Guardian reported the memo amid public scrutiny of three detainee deaths, reports of harsh conditions and a measles outbreak that had placed detainees in quarantine. DHS said it was reviewing the facility and that no decision had been made about terminating or extending the contract. The memo provided no reason or timeline, and it did not say the facility itself would close.

The Washington Post corrected its initial headline and reported on March 11 that ICE terminated the contractor’s agreement but planned to keep Camp East Montana operating with another company. The Texas Tribune likewise reported that ICE replaced the operator while the facility remained open. The event was therefore a planned contract termination and contractor change, not closure of the detention camp. The sources connect the proposed change to a period of intense criticism, but do not establish that the criticism or outbreak caused the contract decision.
evidence_notes: The Guardian/WaPo describe a memo about ending the operator’s contract and quote DHS saying no decision had been made. Washington Post correction states the March 11 contract termination did not close the camp, which remained open under a new contractor. The initial closure headline was inaccurate.
corrected_wording: Corrected the event from a reported facility closure to contract termination/operator replacement, and incorporated the confirmed outcome that the facility stayed open.
